chapterNote: At the second banquet the mask comes off. Esther names the plot, names her people as its target, and names the man — 'this wicked Haman.' In a matter of minutes the schemer is exposed, condemned, and hanged on the very gallows he built for Mordecai. The enemy is caught in his own trap, and the deliverance the fast had sought is granted at a dinner table.

1.text: So the king and Haman came to dine with Queen Esther.

2.text: And again, on this second day, as they drank their wine, the king said, "What is your petition, Queen Esther? It will be granted. What is your request? Even to half the kingdom, it will be done."

3.text: Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favor in your eyes, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be granted me at my petition, and my people at my request.
3.notes: Esther finally lifts the veil she has kept since the harem: to plead for 'my people' is to confess she is one of them. Her own life and her people's are now bound in a single appeal — she stakes her queenship on being counted a Jew.

4.text: For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, killed, and annihilated. Had we merely been sold as slaves, men and women, I would have held my peace — such a wrong would not have been worth troubling the king."
4.notes: Her words deliberately echo Haman's decree (3:13) — 'destroyed, killed, and annihilated' — turning his own language into the indictment. And her restraint is pointed: only extermination, not mere hardship, has driven her to break the law of the unsummoned approach.

5.text: Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, "Who is he? Where is the man who has dared to do such a thing?"

6.text: "A foe, an enemy — this wicked Haman!" said Esther. And Haman stood terrified before the king and queen.

7.text: In a rage the king rose from the wine and went out into the palace garden, while Haman stayed to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he saw that the king had already settled on his ruin.

8.text: When the king came back from the palace garden into the banquet hall, Haman had thrown himself down on the couch where Esther reclined. "Will he even assault the queen while I am in the house?" the king said. As the words left his mouth, they covered Haman's face.
8.notes: The man who would destroy a people is undone in a moment of misread desperation: his plea for mercy looks like an assault, and the covering of his face marks him as a condemned man. The one who cast lots to control a nation's fate has lost all control of his own.

9.text: Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs attending the king, said, "Look — the gallows Haman made for Mordecai, whose word once saved the king, stands at Haman's house, seventy-five feet high." "Hang him on it," said the king.

10.text: So Haman was hanged on the very gallows he had raised for Mordecai, and the king's rage was stilled.
10.amp: they hanged Haman on the gallows [ets — the very tree] he had readied for Mordecai; and the king's wrath was quieted.
10.notes: The perfect reversal the book has been building toward: the trap springs on its maker. 'He digs a pit and falls into the hole he has made' (Ps. 7:15). Haman dies on his own scaffold, and the wrath that sealed a genocide is spent on the man who devised it.
